# Introduction

## Project Overview

AI is often discussed as models, benchmarks, and chatbots.

But the current boom is also a physical infrastructure story:

- **Money:** billions in capital spending
- **Energy:** large new power demands
- **Water:** resource stress around where data centers are built

> **Central question:** How can visualization help people reason about the infrastructure behind the AI boom?

::: {.notes}
When people talk about AI, the conversation usually starts with models:
which model is smartest, which benchmark it beats, or what it can do in a
chat interface. But the recent AI boom is not only a software story. It is also
becoming a physical infrastructure story.

Behind those models are data centers, chips, power contracts, cooling systems,
land, and very large capital investments. Our project is focused on that layer:
the infrastructure behind AI growth. We are not evaluating model performance;
we are trying to make the scale and geography of the buildout more visible.

To make that manageable, we organize the story around three dimensions: money,
energy, and water. The central question is how visualization can help people
reason across those dimensions. That makes this a visualization problem.
:::

## Visualization challenges

- **Multiple dimensions:** money, energy, and water need to be read together
- **Mismatched datasets:** each source captures only part of the picture
- **Geography matters:** sites connect to local grids and water conditions
- **Actors matter:** owners, users, and tenants shape the financial story

**Design task:** connect what is being built, where it is located, who is behind it, and which resources are under pressure.

::: {.notes}
The main visualization challenge is that no single chart or dataset tells the
whole story.

Money, energy, and water are related, but they behave differently. Capital
spending has a time dimension and connects to owners, investors, and tenants.
Energy and water are more geographic: the same data center can look very
different depending on local grid or water-stress conditions.

The data sources also do not line up perfectly. One source may tell us about
frontier AI data centers, another about water stress, and another about
electricity capacity. So our design task is to help the audience hold those
pieces together without overwhelming them.

The rest of the presentation shows how we moved from simpler exploratory views
toward charts that start connecting these dimensions more clearly.
:::

# Evolution so far

We started with an [exploratory report](exploratory-report.qmd) of rough,
self-contained charts. Each round of critique drove a refinement. Four arcs
tell that story:

1. Simple summaries
2. Static exploration -> interactive analysis
3. Water: layering geography incrementally

::: {.notes}
- Even before the exploratory report there were rougher prototypes: raw-table
  widgets, simple one-off visualizations, and a single-summary-statistic
  dashboard, all still linked from the report's "Preliminary exploration"
  section.
- The report recorded "what could be improved" notes under every chart —
  those notes are literally the backlog that produced the current dashboard.
:::

## Static exploration  to interactive analysis

- Early scatters answered exactly one question each, for us
- The refined charts let the *audience* interrogate them: legend-bound
  highlighting, tooltips, and reference lines
- Interactivity became practical after we enabled VegaFusion and fixed the
  renderer to coexist with Observable JS cells

::: {.notes}
The interaction on the next "after" slide: click an owner in the legend to
highlight that owner's sites; the dashed rule marks the median compute
density so the audience can anchor comparisons.
:::

## Before: a one-question scatter


## After: interactive — click a legend entry


## Evolving towards geo viz

The water story was built up one layer at a time, following the exploratory
report's own improvement notes:


```{python}
#| label: evolution-water-choropleth
charts.datacenters.us_state_concentration().properties(width=750, height=430)
```

::: {.notes}

- In our exploratory visualization, start with straightforward bar chart
- Very simple to answer "in what US states are data centers most concentrated"?
- But for understanding resource constraints - power and water availability - we want to tap into geographic and political intuition.
- So, we brough in data on "water stress" and  overlay the AI data centers on it

:::

## Water stress choropleth with AI data centers overlay

```{python}
#| label: evolution-water-comparison
(
    charts.water.baseline_stress_with_datacenters().properties(width=400, height=280)
    | charts.water.future_stress_with_datacenters().properties(width=400, height=280)
)
```

::: {.notes}

- Within the choropleth, power capacity of data center is encoded as size of dot
- Position is used to encode actual approximate geographic location
- A temporal element is introduced - past vs future
- Can roughly understand via dot density the concentration we had seen with the bars
- Future improvment: combine the concentration bar chart with the choropleth via brushing

:::

## Adding energy - additional dimensions

```{python}
#| label: evolution-electricity
charts.electricity.electricity_capacity_with_datacenters().properties(width=750, height=430)
```

::: {.notes}

- Since the power dimension is so important, we wanted to join another data source for power
- Because electric grids are often somewhat characteristic of a state, encode overall capacity for a state as color
- Continue using position of circle marks for actual geographic position
- Continue using size of dots for individual data center capacity

:::

## Testing Plan

- Plan to conduct a usability study with 12 test subjects (recorded over Zoom),
  with the goal of understanding whether our visualizations are successful in
  enabling users to understand the presented data and perform key tasks
- Ask to record each session, take notes during, and review recording and summarize takeaways within 24 hours

## Testing Plan: key things we want to understand

- Does the user understand what they are looking at?
- Are features such as hover tooltips accessible?
- Are the three dimensions of the problem space overwhelming?
- How can we improve the information around the visualizations to clarify the
  narrative and reduce user short-term memory load?

## Testing Plan: example tasks

- Identify which state currently has the highest AI data center power
  consumption
- Compare the difference in power capacity between Ohio and Idaho
- Compare the correlation between capital cost and data center power capacity
- How many sites make up Google's AI data center portfolio?
- Identify Texas's water scarcity score
